comparison: Perfect alignment on Left fast/Right slow split-belt findings (C47, C48, C74-C80). Both evaluations find these results well-supported. OpenEval emphasizes statistical support and rehabilitation implications, while peer reviewers affirm the model's convincing predictive capability for split-belt conditions without disputing these specific findings.

Strong agreement on the core hypothesis about speed-dependent interlimb interactions (C5, C6, C36, C37). OpenEval rates this as SUPPORTED, noting the hypothesis is logically derived and testable. Peer Reviewer 1 explicitly highlights this as a strength, praising insights about left-right spinal network interactions and their speed-dependence.

Divergent evaluations of mechanistic explanations (C84, C85, C87, C91, C92). OpenEval rates these as UNCERTAIN, noting they are inferences rather than directly tested hypotheses and require additional validation. In contrast, Peer Reviewer 2 explicitly praises these mechanisms as 'super cool' and Reviewer 1 values the insights about network interactions, with no challenges raised.

Agreement on model limitations (C95-C98). Both evaluations find these appropriately acknowledged. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting honest assessment of scope. Peer reviewers accept these limitations without dispute, with Reviewer 2 specifically affirming plasticity modeling as an important future direction.

Agreement on model architecture and hemisection implementation (C21-C31, C103, C104). OpenEval finds the model description well-supported with appropriate citations and clear methodology. Peer Reviewer 1 validates the approach, noting as a strength that only connections were altered without parameter adjustments, successfully replicating experimental findings.

Agreement on Left slow/Right fast split-belt results (C42-C46, C69-C72). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with appropriate statistical tests, noting the key finding about swing exceeding stance and increased asymmetry. Peer reviewers affirm these findings are not challenged, with the editor noting convincing evidence and reviewers confirming model-data match.

Divergent evaluations of clinical applications (C102). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting this is aspirational rather than demonstrated and requires clinical trials. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, with the editor calling the study 'important' for researchers working on motor dysfunction after SCI, and Reviewer 1 emphasizing the model's utility as an investigative tool.

Agreement on model's predictive capability (C7, C81, C101). Both evaluations find strong support for qualitative agreement between model and experiment. OpenEval notes this is demonstrated across multiple conditions. All three peer reviewers affirm the model's predictive capability, with the editor providing 'convincing evidence' and reviewers noting the model replicates findings 'very well.'

Agreement on belt configuration effects (C8, C89, C90). OpenEval groups these with other summary claims and rates as SUPPORTED, noting support from both simulation and experimental data. Peer reviewers do not explicitly critique these findings, with the editor's statement about 'convincing evidence' for split-belt predictions encompassing these results.

Agreement on tied-belt experimental results (C39, C40, C59, C60). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting qualitative agreement between simulations and experiments with appropriate statistical tests. Peer reviewers do not challenge these findings, with the editor affirming convincing evidence for predictions about swing and stance alterations at different speeds.

Agreement on model-experiment discrepancy regarding stance duration (C61). OpenEval acknowledges this discrepancy in R4 but notes it doesn't undermine overall patterns. Peer reviewers accept this discrepancy as acknowledged by authors, with the editor noting the model provides 'qualitative' predictions, implicitly accepting some quantitative differences.

Agreement on stance duration discrepancy (C73). OpenEval notes in R5 that this discrepancy doesn't undermine the overall pattern of increased asymmetry findings. Peer reviewers similarly accept this discrepancy without dispute, consistent with their acceptance of qualitative rather than quantitative prediction accuracy.

OpenEval evaluates background knowledge and context claims (C1-C3, C12-C16) as SUPPORTED, noting well-accepted background with appropriate citations and proper identification of knowledge gaps. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these introductory/background claims.

OpenEval evaluates experimental methods (C49-C51, C105-C116) as SUPPORTED, noting clear descriptions, appropriate ethical approval, adequate sample sizes, and reproducible methodology with appropriate statistical methods. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these methodological claims.
